analysis.one_liner: Lets employers refuse to hire job applicants who are working to unionize workplaces.
analysis.headline: Backed by 28 Senate Republicans, the bill held one committee hearing in June 1997, was never reported to the full Senate, and died without a vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Union organizers sometimes apply for jobs at nonunion companies — a tactic called "salting" — so they can work alongside employees and help them form a union. This bill would amend federal labor law to say no employer can be required to hire someone who applied to advance the goals of an organization other than the company, such as a union. Employers could then legally turn away union organizers without violating the ban on anti-union discrimination.
analysis.who_benefits: Employers, especially nonunion companies, would gain the explicit legal right to refuse employment to union organizers, removing a tool unions use to start organizing drives at workplaces where no union exists.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a provision to the National Labor Relations Act stating that nothing in its prohibitions on unfair labor practices requires an employer to hire a person who sought the job to further the objectives of another organization, such as a union.

The bill's findings describe salting — union organizers infiltrating a targeted employer's workplace — as an aggressive practice that threatens the balance of rights in collective bargaining, and say employers should be able to expect applicants to be interested in the employer's business.

analysis.who_pays: Workers who want to organize a union would bear the cost: a lawful organizing method would be taken off the table, making it harder for employees at nonunion companies to win union representation and the wages and conditions that can come with it.

drawbacks.text: The bill would remove one of the few established methods for starting a union campaign at a nonunion workplace, since organizers have no other way to gain access to workers inside a plant or store that a union does not represent.

Because an employer could argue any pro-union applicant was really there to serve an outside organization, the provision would be hard to distinguish from ordinary anti-union hiring discrimination, which the bill's own text says remains prohibited.

The bill's stated purpose claims it preserves employees' rights to organize, but the only practical effect on organizing is to give employers a new legal shield against a tactic used to exercise that right.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Employers would get a clear rule shielding them from having to hire people they believe are organizing on a union's behalf, which addresses a real frustration companies describe. But the cost falls on workers' legal right to organize: salting has long been treated as protected activity under the National Labor Relations Act, and this bill would sharply narrow it. On balance, the bill trades a genuine workplace-organizing tool for employer convenience, and its protections against view-based discrimination would be difficult to enforce in practice.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the Senate labor committee, which held a single hearing in June 1997 and never voted to send it to the floor, and it died when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 13, 1997 by Sen. Tim Hutchinson with 16 original cosponsors, and 27 Republicans cosponsored in total.
The Senate referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources, which held hearings on June 10, 1997 — the bill's only recorded action beyond introduction.
The committee never reported the bill to the Senate, and no floor vote was ever held; the Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers and unions came out ahead: the salting tactic remains lawful, and employers did not get the new right to screen out union organizers. Employers who backed the bill gained nothing from its death.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Union organizers and workers seeking to unionize

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat signed on.

sides.party_line_note: All 28 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never reached a floor vote where party positions could be tested.

industries.note: The bill would have given employers an explicit legal right to refuse to hire union organizers, removing a tactic used to help their employees unionize. Its death left employers without that shield.

industries.industry: Labor unions and professional union organizers
industries.note: Salting is a primary way unions gain access to workers at nonunion firms; the bill would have made such organizers unemployable at the companies they target. Its defeat preserved the tactic.
